body:
# Independent audit of exposed-fiber compression and real interpolation

The following two notes pass in their stated scopes:

- `candidate 25f2a08c9ca43383`;
- `candidate f7422e63e37f7d98`.

No general OC conclusion follows from either restricted statement.

## 1. Closed full-fiber cover extraction

The minimax certificate is valid on any compact convex full-dimensional
fiber, including a minimizing point on its boundary. Its active cap
values are all the common minimum of their maximum. Caratheodory
reduction of their weighted continuous normal preserves the weighted
affine value because those active values agree at the minimizing point.
Thus at most d+1 original restrictions really cover every point of the
fiber. This correctly avoids replacing closed-cap coverage by an
unjustified Helly statement for open complements.

If a retained cap covers the whole body, keeping only that cap still
covers. If no retained cap does, a zero-volume cap contains no interior
point: a nonzero affine normal through any interior point cuts a
positive-volume half-ball. The remaining finite union of closed caps
therefore covers the interior and its closure, which is the whole
fiber. All remaining cap volumes are strictly between zero and the
fiber volume. A closed cap missing a point cannot have full volume,
since its open complement then intersects a positive-volume interior
cone of the body.

## 2. Median replacement and global accounting

For a whole-fiber cap with local threshold t, t is at most the minimum
of its continuous projection. A median m gives two proper half-volume
caps. The absolute-deviation minimum gives

    integral |X-m|<=integral |X-t|=integral(X-t)_+.

The symmetric difference body satisfies h_D(-u)=h_D(u), so this is
exactly the required comparison of normalized hinges, not just their
unnormalized numerators. Both new cap masses are at most the original
whole-fiber mass and hence at most its original global cap budget.
The replacement uses two caps, which is at most d+1 even when d=1.

Exposing a base vertex by q_z and multiplying it by a sufficiently
large finite coefficient leaves the chosen local margin unchanged and
makes it strictly negative on every other compact fiber. This preserves
the continuous normal, denominator, own-fiber mass and own-fiber hinge.

The nonincrease of the total hinge is also valid when one original cap
was selected on several fibers: each selection is charged only against
that cap's original integral on its own fiber. Those integrals are
disjoint summands of the original total. The median step is charged
against just the selected whole-fiber summand. No original global cap
budget is added multiple times to justify a new cap's budget.

Each resulting proper cap has positive margin bounded by its own
fiber width, which is at most h_D(u). Thus its normalized hinge is at
most its cap mass. Summing by fiber and alternatively by cap proves
both claimed upper bounds with their exact constants.

## 3. The lattice cardinality and interval optimum

The count |P|<=2^n requires the two stated conditions: all points of P
are vertices, AND P=conv(P) intersect Z^n. Distinct same-parity points
would have an integer midpoint in P, and that midpoint cannot be a
vertex. This works in lower-dimensional affine projections as well;
no lattice normalization is used. Without lattice convexity, the
cardinality assertion is not claimed.

For intervals, dividing each cap by its continuous-normal magnitude
reduces its local normalized cost to a +/-1 hinge divided by W, the
maximum interval length. Keeping the largest upper cap and largest
lower cap preserves coverage and only removes nonnegative hinge terms.
A whole-interval cap costs at least w^2/2; otherwise the two proper
thresholds obey l<=t<=s<=r and cost at least w^2/4, with equality at
the common midpoint. Thus the exact minimum sum w_z^2/(4W) is correct.
Any available cover has a cap containing the longest interval's
midpoint, so its budget is at least W/2. This makes the isolated
midpoint-pair construction budget-feasible and proves attained equality
over all finite cap counts, not just a local comparison.

## 4. Exact interpolation for one integer coordinate

Actual convex compatibility implies h_Kj(u) is a concave sequence for
EVERY continuous covector u, not just for a preferred set of normals.
Its piecewise-linear interpolant is therefore concave. The support of
any convex combination of integer-fiber points at real base s is at
most that interpolant by scalar Jensen. The adjacent Minkowski
interpolation attains the same support. Compact convex sets are
determined by all their supports, proving the exact fiber identity.

The resulting real-fiber widths interpolate linearly between adjacent
integer widths. Their supremum in each direction equals the maximum
integer width, proving D_all(C_*)=D_int. The union of same-real-base
differences is already compact convex because it is the vertical
section of C_*-C_*; no extra convexification changes this argument.

The replacement C_*=conv(S) preserves all actual integer fibers under
the note's explicit assumption that all nonempty fibers are included.
It need not preserve original real fibers. The rectangle with two
large real-base bulges gives precisely the stated obstruction to
claiming D_all(C)=D_int for the original body. The a=b case is a
single fiber and satisfies both identities directly.

## 5. Affine sections, factor two, and an integer core

For a common affine section c on aff(P), first extend c affinely to
R^n if its original domain is proper. Such an extension exists by
extending a basis of its affine direction space. The shear
x -> x-c(z) then preserves every integer base and all same-base
differences. Every translated integer fiber contains zero, so lies
in its own difference body and hence in D_int. Every real fiber of
their convex hull also lies in D_int. Subtracting two such points
gives D_all subset D_int-D_int=2D_int. The binary-square example
attains factor two exactly. A simplex projection supplies the affine
section by choosing one point in each vertex fiber and interpolating;
actual convex compatibility guarantees all other indexed memberships.

For the radial-core condition, p-z0 in R(z0-conv(P)) gives the stated
real q with z0=(p+Rq)/(1+R). One fixed point of the real q-fiber and
convexity put a translated (1+R)^(-1) copy of the entire real p-fiber
inside the actual integer fiber K_z0. Taking differences proves the
factor 1+R exactly, including lower-dimensional base projections. No
dimension-only estimate of R is assumed.

## 6. Trace clipping and minor wording precisions

The proper central half-interval forces the clipping cap's continuous
normal to be +1 and its offset zero. Covering the z=1 interval forces
A>=1/2; exact pointwise exclusion at z=-1 forces strict inequality,
which only strengthens the displayed lower bound. The central hinge
is 1/8 and the positive-fiber integrals are Aj, giving exactly
1/8+N(N+1)/4. The mass remains M/2 and the normalized hinge diverges.
The horizontal pair has total hinge M/4, so it is bounded RELATIVE
TO M; that qualification removes possible ambiguity in the phrase
'bounded hinge.' This is a wording precision, not a gap in the claim.

Likewise, before the lattice assumption is imposed, the compression
theorem allows P subset R^n. References there to 'integer fibers'
can simply be read as 'indexed fibers'; the proof itself uses no
integrality until the final parity count. These terminology points
do not affect the correctness or the exact constants.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
